citation: docs/architecture.md, one action path: every surface sends the same Request, so a CLI is a way of spelling one rather than a second set of behaviours. The words a command line uses are Muster's own policy and there is no oracle above them; what each field means is documented on the messages themselves in proto/muster.proto. kan a_26BJb2n6o and a_294MvlG1E.
why: What `muster pane new --down --run claude` becomes is the whole contract between an agent and the window it is sitting in, and it is the part that outlives this implementation - a `muster` rewritten in anything else has to turn the same words into the same requests. Three shapes of outcome are pinned: the request a line becomes, the refusal a line earns from us, and the *kind* of complaint clap makes about a line it cannot read. The kind rather than the wording, because the wording is clap's and would change under a version bump, while `an unknown flag is refused rather than swallowed` is the promise. Fields left at their protobuf default are absent here, so a case reads as what somebody actually said: `side` and a rename's `name` are the exceptions, the first because every split has a side and the default is the point, and the second because an empty name is what takes a name away.

cases.name: the whole window is one read
cases.why: An agent has no eyes, so this is half the value of the surface. One request rather than a question per pane, because a caller that has to ask again for each cannot see them at one moment.

cases.name: a split with no side lands to the right
cases.why: Right is where cmd+d puts one, and the CLI and the keyboard have to agree about what `a split` means - a default that matched no chord would make the same word mean two things depending on which surface you used.

cases.name: a pane made from inside a pane splits the one it is running in
cases.why: The mechanism the whole scenario rests on: an agent told to split two panes below itself names no pane, and MUSTER_PANE is the only thing that can say which one it is. Muster puts it in the environment of the very request that creates the pane.

cases.name: a named pane beats the one this is running in
cases.why: An agent arranging panes for others addresses them by name while sitting in its own, so the flag has to win. If the environment won, an integrator could only ever act on itself.

cases.name: an exported but empty MUSTER_PANE is not an answer
cases.why: An exported-but-empty variable is a normal state of a shell profile, and of a herdr pane restored after a daemon restart - those get no launch environment at all. Read as a real answer it would send a request naming the pane called `""`, which no window holds, instead of falling through to the pane the keyboard is on.

cases.name: a pane made for an agent carries its program and its name
cases.why: The gesture the cards are about, in one line. Both travel with the split rather than as requests afterwards: the program because a caller sending it itself would race the new shell's first prompt, and the name because a rename arriving later leaves the pane briefly nameless in every window showing it.

cases.name: a pane can be asked for on a machine rather than beside a pane
cases.why: The only way to reach a machine you have no pane on, which is every devenv on the day it is attached and any machine whose last pane you closed. Every other route to a new pane goes through an existing one - a split inherits its pane's machine, a tab takes the workspace from a pane - so without this a machine that reaches zero panes is one nothing in Muster can put a pane back on. The side still travels, because a machine already showing panes splits the one its region has the keyboard on.

cases.name: a machine named from inside a pane does not carry that pane
cases.why: The case that would silently do the opposite of what was asked. $MUSTER_PANE is sent whenever nobody names a pane, and the window reads a named pane as the whole address - so a `--daemon` that let the environment through would send the request straight back to the machine it was trying to leave, and would look like it worked. clap refuses --pane beside --daemon; only this side can refuse the pane nobody typed.

cases.name: the keyboard moves only when asked
cases.why: take_focus is absent from every other case here, and that is the point: an agent opening three panes would otherwise drag somebody's cursor through all three. Pressing a key means `I made this and I am looking at it`; a script means `make it and leave my cursor alone`.

cases.name: an empty --run is nothing to run
cases.why: A script interpolating a variable that turned out empty would otherwise ask the window to wait for a prompt and then type nothing, which costs the readiness wait and leaves a pane looking like it failed at something.

cases.name: text that asks for a return is submitted
cases.why: The other half of an agent instructing another. Return is a flag rather than a newline in the text because the two differ once a program is reading: Return is encoded against the pane's live modes, and a bare newline inside a bracketed paste is text rather than a submission.

cases.name: asking to be sure the text arrived is a third thing the send carries
cases.why:
Not a second command, and that is the point of it being a flag. A caller that sent and then read the pane itself would be two requests with a gap between them, and the gap is where a harness redraws - so the check has to be part of the send and the window has to make it.

It is independent of `--enter`, because the two answer different questions. `--enter` asks for a Return; this asks whether the message can be seen on the pane afterwards. A caller that wants a message left sitting on a prompt still wants to know it got there.

cases.name: text with no return waits on the prompt
cases.why: The difference between telling an agent something and leaving a line sitting there for a person to look at. Both are wanted, so the flag has to be the only thing that decides.

cases.name: unquoted text arrives in pieces and is sent as one line
cases.why: Somebody typing an instruction will forget the quotes, and joining is what they meant - the alternative is a refusal for a command line with exactly one possible reading. Single spaces, because the shell already ate whatever else was between the words.

cases.name: a double dash makes text of something that looks like a flag
cases.why: Instructions to an agent contain flags. Without this there would be no way to send the characters `--enter` to a pane, and the failure would be silent: the flag would be honoured and the text would go out one word shorter than it was written.

cases.name: renaming a pane says what to call it
cases.why: A person running fifteen agents wants to say which is which in their own words, and this is the surface a script sets those names from.

cases.name: an empty name takes the name away
cases.why: One spelling for `no name` rather than two, and the only way to undo a rename. Absence and the empty string have to stay distinguishable here, which is why this field is written out even when it is empty.

cases.name: closing with nothing named closes the pane this is running in
cases.why: Consistent with every other command, and worth pinning precisely because it is the surprising one: an agent that runs this ends the shell its own process is in. The help says so; this makes sure the behaviour matches what the help says.

cases.name: focus with nothing named goes to the pane this is running in
cases.why: An agent asking to be looked at, which is the one thing in this vocabulary that reaches for a person's attention rather than for a pane.

cases.name: focus with nothing to focus is refused rather than sent
cases.why: The one command where an empty pane is not an answer: everywhere else the window reads it as `the pane the keyboard is on`, and asking to focus the focused pane is not something to ask for. Refused here rather than at the window, because only out here is it known that the reason is a missing MUSTER_PANE - the window would only be able to say that no pane was named.

expect.refused: `muster focus` needs a pane, a direction or a place, and $MUSTER_PANE is not set - so this is not running inside a pane Muster made. Name one: `muster focus p1w3r07bsd`, or say `--next`. `muster window` lists them.

cases.name: zoom with nothing named means the pane the keyboard is on
cases.why: Run from a terminal outside Muster there is no MUSTER_PANE, and the useful answer is still `the pane somebody is looking at`. The empty pane id is how every request in the schema spells that, so this sends one rather than refusing.

cases.name: an answer can be asked for as JSON
cases.why: The flag every command takes, and the one an agent always passes. It changes the rendering and never the request, which is what lets the two renderings come from one answer.

cases.name: a window can be named instead of looked for
cases.why: The escape hatch for a caller that is not in a pane and has more than one Muster open, which would otherwise be refused with nothing to do about it.

cases.name: a flag nobody has is refused rather than ignored
cases.why: The commonest mistake an agent makes, and the one that must not pass quietly: a swallowed `--focused` would be a pane that appeared somewhere nobody expected with no sign that anything was wrong.

cases.name: two sides at once is refused
cases.why: A pane lands on one side of another, so there is no honest thing to do with both - and picking one silently would be picking for somebody who has said they are unsure.

cases.name: a pane and a machine are two answers to one question
cases.why: A pane's name is already unique across every machine the window shows, so naming a machine beside one is either a restatement or a contradiction - and there is no way to tell which from out here. Refused rather than resolved, on the same terms as a pane and a direction for `focus`.

cases.name: a verb that does not exist is refused
cases.why: Every word in this vocabulary is one somebody typed from memory. A misspelling has to come back as a refusal naming the verbs there are, rather than as nothing happening.

cases.name: a rename with no name is refused
cases.why: Distinct from the empty name above, which is a deliberate ask. Nothing at all is somebody who has not finished typing, and taking the name away would be the wrong guess at what they meant.

cases.name: a pane name where a window subcommand goes is refused
cases.why: `muster window p1w3r07bsd` reads like a request to describe one pane, and there is no such request. Answering the whole window instead would look like it had been narrowed and had not. Refused as an unknown subcommand rather than a stray argument since `window` grew `list` and `new` under it, which is the more useful of the two complaints: it names what may go there.

cases.name: nothing at all shows what there is
cases.why: A bare `muster` is somebody finding out what this is, so it prints the help rather than complaining about an absence. It still exits non-zero, because nothing was asked and nothing happened.

cases.name: a tab is gone to by name
cases.why: The command the whole card exists for. Before it, a script could read a tab out of `muster window` and had no way to act on it - focusing a pane in the tab was the only route, which means knowing a pane in it. No daemon travels: a tab name is unique across every attached machine, so the window finds which one holds it.

cases.name: going to a tab needs one named
cases.why: Where a pane command falls back to $MUSTER_PANE, this refuses. There is no equivalent for a tab - nothing tells a pane which tab holds it - and `the tab the keyboard is in` is not somewhere to ask to go. Refused by clap rather than here, because a missing positional is exactly what clap is for and its message names the argument.

cases.name: a tab is renamed by name
cases.why: The other half. An agent that made a tab for its own work names it so the person at the keyboard can tell it apart, exactly as it names a pane - and it has to say which tab, because the keyboard is somewhere else.

cases.name: renaming with no tab means the tab the keyboard is in
cases.why: The empty field, which the schema reads as the tab holding the pane the window's keyboard is on - what the menu item means. Deliberately not the tab this command is running in: nothing in a pane's environment says which tab holds it, and guessing from $MUSTER_PANE would need a second round trip from a parser that is pure by design.

cases.name: an empty name takes a tab's name away
cases.why: The same spelling a pane's rename uses, so one rule covers both: an empty name is the request to go back to being unnamed. How completely that happens is the backend's answer - herdr leaves the tab holding an empty label rather than restoring its number - and the caption then draws the place.

cases.name: a tab is closed by name
cases.why: The verb that was missing: Close Pane existed and emptying a tab one pane at a time was the only route to the same place. A tab name is Muster's own and unique across every machine, so no daemon travels with it.

cases.name: closing with no --tab closes the tab this is running in
cases.why: The fallback going to a tab deliberately does not have. `tab focus` with no tab means nothing - there is no `the one I am already in` to go to - and closing one is exactly that, which is what a menu item means by it.

cases.name: a tab verb that does not exist is refused
cases.why:
`muster tab` has fewer verbs than `muster pane`, and the ones it lacks it lacks for a reason: nothing types into a tab, and nothing reads one. Somebody will try anyway, and a refusal that lists what there is beats a request nobody can build.

This case used to be `tab close`, on the argument that a tab closes when its last pane does. That argument was wrong about what it cost: emptying a tab one pane at a time was the only route to a thing people do, so `tab close` exists now (kan `a_2Ic6mB36E`) and the case moved to a verb that really has no meaning for a tab.

cases.name: a tab is made beside the pane this is running in
cases.why: The other way to make a pane, and until now the one thing a script could not do: splitting was the only route, so anything that did not belong in this tab had nowhere to go. No pane is named, so the tab joins the workspace of the pane this is running in - the same answer cmd+T means by naming nothing.

cases.name: a tab made for an agent carries its program and its name
cases.why: The same intention `pane new --run --name` carries, for the same reason: the program travels with the tab because a caller sending it afterwards would race the new shell's prompt, and the name travels because a rename arriving later leaves the pane briefly nameless. A tab that could be made and not equipped would send every caller back to splitting.

cases.name: making a tab does not move the keyboard
cases.why: The rule `pane new` already follows, restated because a tab is the louder case: it comes on screen either way, so the only question is whether somebody's cursor goes with it. An agent opening three tabs must not drag it through all three.

cases.name: a tab can be made on a machine rather than beside a pane
cases.why: The same reach as `pane new --daemon`, and on a machine holding nothing the two mean the same thing: a tab lives in a workspace and a machine with no pane has none, so both become the one request that makes a workspace. Spelled on both verbs because a caller reaches for whichever noun they want, and a surface where only one of them could say `over there` would be a rule to remember rather than a rule.

cases.name: a tab is stepped to rather than named
cases.why: The other axis to stepping panes: `focus --next` reaches every pane the window is showing, and this reaches the tabs behind them. A script that has read one tab out of `muster window` can walk the rest without reading again.

cases.name: a tab cannot be both named and stepped to
cases.why: Two answers to one question. Naming a tab and asking for the next one are different intentions, and honouring either silently would be picking for somebody who said both.

cases.name: a tab cannot be asked for both beside a pane and on a machine
cases.why: The same refusal on the other verb. Both are spelled the same way and both have to refuse the same way, or the rule is one people learn per command.

cases.name: a pane is moved onto another
cases.why: The verb the card is about. The window works out which of the two things this means from where the panes are - the same tab is an exchange, another tab is a move - so one verb here rather than two, and no daemon travels: a pane name is unique across every attached machine.

cases.name: moving with no --pane moves the pane this is running in
cases.why: The rule every pane verb follows, and worth pinning here because moving names two panes and could plausibly have demanded both. An agent asking to be put beside another agent should not have to look up its own name first.

cases.name: moving a pane needs somewhere to put it
cases.why: The half that has no default. Where a pane goes is the whole content of the request, and there is no `the obvious place` for the window to fall back to.

cases.name: a pane is moved into a tab of its own
cases.why: The other destination, and the reason the verb needed one: pulling a pane out of a split used to take `tab new`, this move, and `pane close` to throw away the shell the first command started - three round trips, not atomic, and the keyboard landing in the throwaway on the way past.

cases.name: a tab a move makes can be named
cases.why: `--name` fills the label on the request. The dance this replaces could not set it at all: it made the tab before anything knew what was going into it, so the name would have had to be a fourth command.

cases.name: moving with --new-tab and no --pane moves the pane this is running in
cases.why: The same fallback the rest of the verb has, and it reaches further here: this destination names one pane rather than two, so an agent asking to be pulled out of a split says nothing at all beyond the flag.

cases.name: a move goes to one place or the other, never both
cases.why: Two destinations in one command line is a caller that means two things, and picking one by precedence would carry out a request nobody wrote. Refused where the position flags on other verbs are refused - by the parser, before anything is sent.

cases.name: naming a tab without asking for one is refused
cases.why: `--name` only means anything with `--new-tab`, and a name silently dropped is a tab that comes back unnamed with nothing saying why. Refused against `--onto` rather than made to require `--new-tab`: a bool flag is present in clap's sense whether or not it was typed, so a requirement on one is a requirement nothing can fail, and the required destination group leaves refusing the other half saying exactly the same thing.

cases.name: a pane is grown by the window's own step
cases.why: What a resize chord means, said from a script. No amount travels, because zero is what the window reads as `your own step` - so a caller with nothing particular in mind gets what the keyboard gets rather than a distance this CLI invented.

cases.name: a divider can be placed exactly
cases.why: The half a chord cannot ask for. A person holds a key down and looks; a script cannot look, so it says how far in one request rather than guessing how many presses that was.

cases.name: resizing needs a direction
cases.why: A resize with no direction is not a smaller request, it is an unfinished one - and unlike a split there is no side that happens anyway to default to.

cases.name: the keyboard steps to the next pane
cases.why: The chord's other door. `next` and `previous` walk reading order across every region and wrap, so between them they reach every pane the window is showing - which is the guarantee the four directions do not make.

cases.name: the keyboard steps geometrically
cases.why: The four directions are about where a pane is on screen rather than where it sits in a list, and they do not wrap. Spelled with the same four words a split uses, so a caller that reads a side out of an answer can send it straight back.

cases.name: a pane is reached by the number drawn beside it
cases.why: `muster window` prints a place for every pane and nothing consumed it until now, which left a number a script could read and not act on. This is cmd+3 from a script.

cases.name: a pane and a direction are two answers to one question
cases.why: Where to put the keyboard has one answer. A name, a direction and a place are three ways of giving it, and two at once is a caller who has not decided.

cases.name: the config file is read again on request
cases.why: The fourth door onto one action: a chord, a menu item, a saved file and this all arrive at the same reload. Worth having from a script because editing the file and applying it are two acts, and a script that writes one wants to finish the job.

cases.name: the agent list is shown or put away
cases.why: A toggle rather than a set, matching what the chord and the menu item send: neither of them knows which way the list currently is, and the window does.

cases.name: text is made bigger in the pane the keyboard is on
cases.why: The window's own three words rather than English ones like `bigger`, on the rule the four sides follow. No pane is named because none can be: the request carries no pane id, and what it means is the pane in front of whoever asked.

cases.name: a font change nobody has is refused
cases.why: Three changes exist and clap knows all three, so a fourth is caught out here with the list beside it rather than by the window with a request already sent.

cases.name: a pane is read back
cases.why: The half of a pane an agent could not see. `muster window` says what state every agent is in and what it claims to be doing, and neither of those is what the pane printed - so an agent watching another one could tell that it had stopped and not why.

cases.name: a read with no rows asks for as much as there is
cases.why: Zero is what the window reads as `as far as you will go`, and it is also what an absent number sends - so a caller with nothing particular in mind and a caller who said nothing make the same request rather than two that have to be kept in agreement.

cases.name: a read can ask for the last few rows only
cases.why: An agent checking whether a command finished wants the bottom of the pane, not a thousand rows of it. Said as a count rather than left to the caller to trim, so the rows never cross the wire.

cases.name: windows are listed without naming one
cases.why: The one read that cannot be narrowed. `--socket` and $MUSTER_SOCKET both mean `this window`, and the question here is which windows there are - so this dials every endpoint rather than the one a caller is standing in, and sends no request that any single window could answer.

expect.answers_here: asking every window on this machine

cases.name: making a window asks no window for it
cases.why: A window is a process, so this starts one rather than sending a request - and it has to, because the case it exists for is having no window to ask. It is the only verb here that is not something the keyboard could send instead.

cases.name: a bare window read is still a read
cases.why: `muster window` kept its meaning when `window` grew subcommands under it. A caller that had this in a script before is asking the same thing after, which is the whole reason the subcommand is optional.

cases.name: a window that was closed is brought back
cases.why:
The gap this closes: New Window made a fresh one and nothing reopened the last, so the only way back to a window you had closed was to rebuild it by hand. Not a request, for the same reason `window new` is not one - a window is a process, so this starts an app rather than asking a running one.

The two differ in what the launched window is told, and the window works that out from the flag it was started with. Which arrangement it takes is not this CLI's decision to make twice.

expect.answers_here: starting the Muster whose window was closed
